metadata.title: Home or School? The Impact of Social Environmental Factors in the Creativity Performance of Primary Education Children

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary data in Spain from 12 schools (903 families; 1052 children) using paper-based questionnaires and a figural creativity task. The methodology reports descriptive statistics and regression/correlation analyses using SPSS v28, but it does not describe the use of complex survey sampling weights or any ILSA-style design weights. Because the analysis is based on a convenience sample of schools and students rather than an international probability sample, no sampling-weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is specified or applied. The analytic sample appears to be the set of children who completed the creativity task and the subset of parents/teachers who returned questionnaires, without any stated weight-based rebalancing.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study’s dependent variable is children’s creativity measured via the Children’s Creativity Test (TCI) total score converted to an age-normative percentile, not an ILSA cognitive achievement scale with Plausible Values. Because the outcome is not PV-based, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation), so missing-data handling is not reported; this is a transparency gap for how questionnaire nonresponse or incomplete tasks were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study analyzed 1052 children aged 6–13 years who completed the Children’s Creativity Test (TCI) in 12 educational centers in Eastern Spain (including public and private schools; urban and rural). Parents/guardians provided questionnaire data for 903 families (967 parent responses; 71.6% mothers, 19.1% fathers, 8.7% both parents), and teachers completed the Teaching for Creativity Scales with 110 teacher participants. The paper does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond participation and completion of the creativity task and questionnaires; it also does not describe any explicit missing-item or nonresponse handling procedure.

main_findings.dataset_used: TCI creativity task (Children’s Creativity Test) in Spanish primary schools (ages 6–13)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical regression: Step 1 (school dummies + EE) R2=0.038, F(12,1039)=3.375, p<0.001; Step 2 adding EENV/ENC/SPCE/EF ΔR2=0.002, F change(4,1034)=0.658, p=0.606; final model R2=0.040, F(16,1035)=2.679, p<0.001. Teacher EE not significant (Step 1: B=0.124, p=0.978; Step 2: B=0.329, p=0.942). Home climate dimensions not significant (all p>0.350). School effects significant vs School 10 (e.g., School 7 B=10.135, p=0.002; School 11 B=13.093, p<0.001). Correlations: no significant correlations between any home climate dimension and creativity (e.g., EENV vs creativity r=-0.068, p=0.027; ENC vs creativity r=-0.124, p<0.001; SPCE vs creativity r=-0.030, p=0.326; EF vs creativity r=-0.016, p=0.609).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the TCI creativity task in Spanish primary schools (ages 6–13) the study leveraged educational center (school dummies) and teacher environmental encouragement (EE) together with home creativity climate dimensions (EENV, ENC, SPCE, EF) to predict children’s creativity percentile score, finding that school context significantly predicted creativity while home creativity climate dimensions did not show significant direct predictive contributions. This indicates that strengthening school-level creativity-supportive cultures and practices may be more actionable than relying on measured home creativity climate dimensions alone, though the convenience-sample design limits generalizability.

data.outcome_summary: This study used primary data from 12 schools in Eastern Spain, analyzing 1052 children aged 6–13 who completed the Children’s Creativity Test (TCI) and 903 families who completed the Climate for Creativity in Parent–Child Relationship Questionnaire (CCP-CRQ), alongside teacher ratings from the Teaching for Creativity Scales (environmental encouragement subscale). The main quantitative results come from correlation and hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS v28), not from machine learning. Children’s overall creativity performance averaged 47.05 (SD=26.71) percentile points, with significant between-school differences (one-way ANOVA H(11,1052)=39.124, p<0.001). In regression, school context plus teacher EE explained 3.8% of variance (R2=0.038), and adding home climate dimensions did not improve prediction (ΔR2=0.002, p=0.606), with all home dimensions non-significant (all p>0.350). Limitations include convenience sampling, reliance on self-report questionnaires, and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
